what: THE COLOSSUS, wave 12, and the one figure on this deck that is NOT a skinned rig. The owner delivered a Meshy PART-SEGMENTATION export - 13 separate geometries - and chose the approach with it: "I feel like if we just do simple segmented movement it might work well for the boss. It's not exactly a humanoid model, and it doesnt move that much, and its death animation could be the parts just falling apart." So there is no skeleton and no skin: each part is a node, each joint is that node's origin, a hinge is a rotation, and the death is the articulation running backwards. Board SG-90.
source: THE OWNER'S OWN MESHY SESSION - a part-segmentation export, not generated by tools/meshy.py, so there is no prompt, no task id and no credit line for it here. The prompted Colossus this replaces is recorded under `superseded` below.
delivered_note: Meshy PART-SEGMENTATION export: 13 separate geometries, no UVs, no texture images, each part flat-filled with a categorical LABEL colour. `label_colour` records the label; `colour` is what the part actually wears, assigned by role out of the project palette.
archived_at: .model_originals/boss_parts/ (outside git and outside Godot's scan, the same place the knight's and the Boilerwright's sources live)
built_by: python tools/segment_parts.py boss <the delivered glb>   - names, budgets, decimates, pivots; writes the kit + parts.json
godot --headless --script tools/rig_parts.gd -- boss     - hierarchy, materials, the five clips; writes boss_parts.scn + boss.tscn
screen_units_note: scripts/view3d.gd `boarder_height("BOSS")` = 120 + radius*3 with no FIGURE_SCALE row. The SIM's own number for the archetype, exactly as the knight's 216 was. handoff-3d/README.md guessed "~360"; the guess was not used.
part_map_note: Which GLTF_n in the delivered file is which limb. Every name was DERIVED from the geometry's own bounds by tools/segment_parts.py - a midline part is a spine part, an outboard chain is an arm, the lowest pair is feet - so a re-export that renumbers the geometries does not silently swap a leg for an arm. +X is the figure's LEFT (it faces +Z with +Y up). `label` is the segmentation colour Meshy shipped the part flat-filled with; both halves of every measured pair share theirs, which corroborates the pairing - though the palette reuses colours across roles (the fists and the feet are the same yellow), so a label can never identify a pair on its own.

decimation.how: fast_simplification (quadric), per part, LOCAL and free
decimation.why_safe: There are NO SKIN WEIGHTS on a rigid part. What makes decimating the captain a standing open decision (board SG-13) is that her weights ride her vertices; a part carries nothing but its own surface, so this cost zero credits and risked nothing.
decimation.budget_source: tools/meshy.py TRI_CEIL - and it is what the PROMPTED Colossus shipped at (see `superseded`), same archetype at the same on-screen height, so this kit got the same budget and not a bigger one.
decimation.split: by surface area, floored at 220 a part, and EQUAL across each mirrored pair so the two sides cannot decimate to different counts.

tex.note: ZERO texture bytes, and that is a property of the delivered file rather than a budget decision: the part-segmentation export carries no UVs and no images at all. Each part wears a flat albedo out of the project palette, assigned by ROLE (see `parts`). The furnace grate the prompted Colossus carried in an emission map cannot be mapped without UVs, so it is a LIGHT instead - the `boss` row in assets/models/lights.json, at the torso's measured front centre, on the furnace knight's flicker.

superseded.note: The prompted Colossus that stood here until 2026-08-02: a Meshy-6 generation, remeshed to 8,000 triangles, wired as a STATIC lump (a plain glb has no AnimationPlayer, so rig3d's `want()` returned early and it never moved). Its file is left in place as the record of the 35 credits it cost; nothing loads it any more.
superseded.prompt: A colossal steampunk siege mech: a vast riveted brass and iron barrel torso with a glowing orange furnace grate at its centre; a tiny domed head with one amber lens; two enormous cannon barrels over the shoulders angled up and outward; huge oversized armoured fists on short arms; thick armoured legs with anchor-shaped feet. One character alone, standing upright, facing forward, feet flat on the ground, arms clear of the body. No base, no plinth, no ground plane, no scenery, no duplicate, no text. Stylised game-ready steampunk airship character: blackened steel, riveted brass fittings, oxblood leather, oxidised copper accents, honest wear at the edges. Chunky readable forms and broad flat colour areas, not photoreal, no micro-detail. Flat albedo, no baked lighting, no baked shadow.
superseded.texture_prompt: Blackened iron plate with heavy polished brass banding and rivets, a hot orange furnace grate, verdigris teal in the seams, bare worn steel around the cannon mouths. Hand-painted stylised game texture: blackened gunmetal, warm polished brass, deep oxblood leather, dull oxidised-copper patina settled in the recesses, bare worn metal along the working edges. Any furnace, grate, vent, ember or lamp flame is hot orange; nothing else emits light. Broad flat colour areas, no baked lighting, no baked shadow, no text, no logos.
